strengths: Addresses a genuinely underexplored and practically relevant problem: applying online RL to long-form writing where verifiable/ground-truth rewards are unavailable, distinguishing it from the well-trodden RLVR literature in math/code.

The three proposed components (margin-aware data selection, pairwise comparison reward, dynamic reference scheduling) are coherent, individually motivated, and the paper provides fairly thorough ablations (Tables 3-6) isolating each component's contribution versus reasonable alternatives (difficulty-based selection, pointwise reward, static reference sets, no/static curriculum).

The dynamic reference scheduling idea—advancing per-sample reference difficulty asynchronously as the policy beats its current reference—is a reasonably novel and computationally cheap way (no extra rollouts) to implement curriculum learning in a non-verifiable-reward setting.

Reasonably strong empirical results across three long-form writing benchmarks and two base model families (Qwen2.5-7B, Llama3.1-8B), showing consistent gains over strong SFT baselines and even parity with larger proprietary models.

The reported generalization from long-output RL training to long-input reasoning (LongBench v2) is an interesting, thought-provoking observation that could motivate follow-up work on the input/output relationship in long-context training.
Good reproducibility support in the appendix: detailed prompts, hyperparameters, and training framework/settings are provided.
weaknesses: No human evaluation anywhere in the paper: both the training reward signal and essentially all evaluation benchmarks rely on LLM-as-judge scoring. Since the policy is explicitly optimized to win pairwise LLM-judged comparisons, the central claim of "improved writing quality" is confounded with the possibility that the model is instead learning to exploit stylistic/length/formatting preferences of the judge models, which is a well-documented failure mode not empirically ruled out here.

Overlap between reward/reference-generation models and evaluation infrastructure raises validity concerns: Qwen-Plus is used both to generate high-quality references/pointwise grading during data selection and as the pairwise judge during RL training; although the paper notes evaluation judges differ, WritingBench's judge is also LLM-based and no controlled analysis is given to rule out judge-family bias inflating scores.

Small and narrow training data (only 1.5k selected samples per dataset) and results reported from a single run per configuration; RL training is known to be high-variance, yet no seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests are reported for any benchmark, weakening claims that observed gains (some quite small, e.g., 1-3 points) are reliable rather than noise.

The long-output-to-long-input generalization claim (Section 5) is interesting but under-supported: the improvements on LongBench v2 are modest and the causal explanation offered is purely intuitive/post-hoc without additional probing experiments (e.g., attention/retrieval analysis, controlled ablations isolating the mechanism), so this should be read as a preliminary observation rather than an established finding.

The data-selection/curriculum pipeline itself requires generating references from four separate strong LLMs (Qwen-Plus, GPT-4o, Claude-3.7, DeepSeek-R1) for every candidate instruction plus multi-dimensional LLM grading — a cost and complexity that is comparable to, or exceeds, the SFT data-construction pipelines the paper criticizes as burdensome, undercutting the stated motivation for RL as a lighter-weight alternative.

Limited scale of experiments (only 7B/8B models) and absence of comparison against other published curriculum/RL methods adapted to writing (the 'None'/'Static' curriculum baselines appear to be self-constructed ablations rather than existing published baselines), making it harder to contextualize the relative advance.
Minor inconsistencies (e.g., text states Llama3.1-8B-Writing-RL average as 87.14 while Table 1 reports 87.40) suggest limited proofreading care.

strengths: Addresses a real and under-explored gap: applying outcome-based RL (rather than SFT alone) to long-form writing, where verifiable rewards are unavailable.

The three proposed components (margin-aware data selection, pairwise comparison reward, dynamic reference scheduling) are individually well-motivated and supported by dedicated ablation experiments (Tables 3-6) that isolate each design choice's contribution.
The pairwise reward design cleverly addresses LLM-judge position bias by deliberately placing model output in the disadvantaged position, simultaneously reducing evaluation cost.

Reasonably comprehensive experimental setup spanning two base model families (Qwen2.5-7B, Llama3.1-8B) and three writing benchmarks (WritingBench, EQ-Bench, LongBench-Write), with comparisons to strong proprietary and open-source baselines.

The observed generalization from long-output RL training to long-input reasoning (LongBench v2) is an interesting and potentially impactful empirical finding that could stimulate follow-up work on the relationship between long-context understanding and generation.

Data selection experiments show a thoughtful contrast between margin-aware (learning-potential-based) and difficulty-prioritized selection, providing some insight transferable beyond this specific task.
weaknesses: Both the training reward and part of the data-selection grading rely on LLM-as-judge (Qwen-Plus, plus its own generated criteria), while the paper's own related-work section acknowledges LLM judges suffer from position and self-enhancement bias; no human evaluation is conducted anywhere in the paper to validate that pairwise/quality judgments reflect true writing quality rather than superficial or judge-specific preferences.

No discussion or empirical check for reward hacking (e.g., length or formatting exploitation) despite the explicit long-form generation setting, which is a plausible confound in RL-optimized long-output tasks.

Results are reported as single runs without variance/seed information, which is a concern given both RL training and LLM-judge-based evaluation are known to be noisy; this limits confidence in the reported gains, especially the smaller margins in ablation tables.

The long-output-to-long-input generalization claim, while interesting, is not rigorously isolated: there is no ablation comparing generic RL training (without the specific curriculum/reward design) on writing to see whether the effect is specific to Writing-RL's design or a general property of RL post-training; the causal explanations offered are speculative rather than tested.

Reproducibility is constrained by heavy dependence on several proprietary API models (GPT-4o, Claude-3.7, Qwen-Plus, DeepSeek R1) for reference generation, judging, and reward computation, which raises cost and access barriers and could yield different reward signals if judge models are updated or swapped, though partial mitigation exists via code release.

There is a minor numerical inconsistency between the text (average score 87.14 for Llama3.1-8B-Writing-RL) and Table 1 (87.40), and a stray internal reference ('Table 3.3') instead of the correct table number, suggesting the paper needs another proofreading pass.

Training data for RL is very small (1.5k samples per dataset, ~400 steps), and model scale is limited to 7-8B; while acknowledged as a limitation, this restricts the strength of claims about the general effectiveness and scalability of the framework.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and practically important gap: extending verifiable-reward RL paradigms to open-ended, non-verifiable long-form writing, where ground truths do not exist.

The three proposed components (margin-aware data selection, pairwise comparison reward, dynamic reference scheduling) are individually well-motivated and each is validated with dedicated, well-designed ablation studies (Tables 3-5, 8).

Extensive experimentation across multiple model families and scales (Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama3.1-8B), three writing benchmarks, and both automatic and human evaluation (Fig. 2), which lends credibility to the main claims of improvement over strong SFT baselines.

Robustness checks are commendable: judge-model swap experiment (Qwen-Plus vs. DeepSeek-V3, Table 7), RL algorithm swap (PPO vs. GRPO), and human-judge agreement analysis (Appendix D.1) all show the gains are not artifacts of a specific judge or optimizer.

The reported output-to-input generalization phenomenon (long-output RL training improving long-input reasoning on LongBench v2) is an interesting and potentially impactful observation, supported by a reasonably careful set of controlled ablations and contamination checks (Appendix C) to rule out trivial explanations.

Good practical reproducibility support: detailed hyperparameters, prompts, and a transparent cost-analysis appendix that documents both one-time dataset construction costs and recurring RL training costs.
weaknesses: Both the training reward signal (LLM-as-judge pairwise comparison) and most evaluation benchmarks rely on LLM judges; although the paper attempts to mitigate this via judge-swap experiments, there remains a risk that the entire pipeline (data selection, reward, and evaluation) shares systematic biases correlated with LLM-judge preferences (e.g., verbosity, stylistic flourish) rather than genuine writing quality gains, which is only partially addressed by the fairly small (100-item) human evaluation.

The training set is quite small (1.5k selected samples per dataset), and while an ablation shows diminishing/negative returns from scaling to 5k, this raises questions about how well the margin-aware selection and dynamic scheduling would generalize to broader writing domains or larger training budgets.

Model scale is capped at 14B; the paper's own limitations section acknowledges this, but the claim of 'SOTA performance at scale' and competitiveness with proprietary models should be read cautiously given this ceiling.

The explanation for the output-to-input generalization phenomenon is largely qualitative/speculative ('generating long-form text requires deep understanding of context'); despite the ablations offered, a rigorous causal mechanism is not established, and the finding rests on a single long-input benchmark (LongBench v2), limiting generality of this secondary claim.

PPO is used with a full critic model (same size as policy), which substantially increases training cost/complexity relative to critic-free methods; although a GRPO variant is reported as comparable, the paper does not deeply analyze compute-efficiency trade-offs between the two despite claiming practical cost-effectiveness.

Statistical rigor is somewhat limited: while standard deviations are reported for some experiments (Tables 3-5), no significance testing is performed across the many close-margin comparisons (e.g., PPO vs. GRPO, static vs. dynamic curriculum), making some fine-grained claims (e.g., 'both showing strong performance') harder to fully substantiate.

The pairwise reward design's deliberate placement of the model response in the disadvantaged (second) position to counter judge position bias is a reasonable heuristic, but its effect on reward calibration/robustness is not rigorously validated against a position-swapped or debiased alternative.

strengths: Addresses a genuine, underexplored problem: adapting RL-with-verifiable-reward-style training to long-form writing, where ground-truth rewards do not exist.

The three proposed components (margin-aware data selection, pairwise comparison reward, dynamic reference scheduling) are individually motivated and each is validated with a dedicated ablation (Tables 3-5), rather than only reporting the combined system.

Broad empirical validation: experiments span multiple backbones (Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama3.1-8B), multiple benchmarks (WritingBench, LongBench-Write, Creative-Writing-Bench), human evaluation, judge-robustness checks (Qwen-Plus vs DeepSeek-V3), and general-capability preservation checks (MMLU, MT-Bench).

Reasonable reproducibility effort: detailed hyperparameters, algorithm pseudocode for the scheduling mechanism, evaluation/reward prompts, and a transparent cost breakdown are provided in the appendix.

The output-to-input generalization finding (long-output RL transferring to long-context reasoning) is an interesting empirical observation, and the authors attempt several controlled checks (continued-SFT control, data/length/topic overlap analysis, judge/reward/curriculum ablations) to argue it is not a trivial artifact.
weaknesses: The entire training and much of the evaluation pipeline (data selection scoring, pairwise reward, curriculum scheduling) is built on LLM-as-judge signals from a small set of models (mainly Qwen-Plus); despite a 0.75 human agreement figure on only 300 samples, this creates a risk that gains partly reflect alignment with a particular judge's stylistic preferences rather than genuine writing-quality improvements.

The output-to-input generalization claim, while intriguing, is evaluated on LongBench v2 where overall accuracy is quite low (around 27-33%, not far from a plausible chance baseline for multiple-choice), and no variance/significance testing is reported for these deltas, making it hard to assess whether the reported gains (e.g., 29.6→31.8) are robust rather than noise.

The explanations offered for *why* long-output RL generalizes to long-input reasoning (Section 5) are largely narrative/post-hoc rather than mechanistically or statistically established, weakening the strength of this headline claim relative to how prominently it is featured.

RL training uses only 1.5k selected samples per dataset, and the margin-aware selection procedure itself depends on generating references from multiple expensive proprietary LLMs (Claude-3.7, GPT-4o), which raises questions about the scalability and independent reproducibility of the pipeline beyond well-resourced labs, despite the cost analysis provided.

Baseline comparisons, while including several recent writing-oriented models, do not clearly benchmark against the most recent/strongest RL-based long-form writing systems beyond LongWriter-Zero, leaving open how much of the improvement is attributable to the specific framework versus generally stronger SFT starting points and datasets.

Novelty of individual components is somewhat incremental relative to existing curriculum-RL and pairwise-preference-reward literature (e.g., difficulty-adaptive selection and preference-based rewards have precedent in reasoning RL and RLHF); the main contribution is largely the combination and application to long-form writing rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.
